passage:
Subject: Friday lunch

Dear Ritu,
I've started this email three times, so I'll say it once and then leave it with you.
At the team lunch on Friday, your phone was on speaker when Dev called, and I heard him say you were "too dumb to book a cab". You laughed and said, "That's just his way, he's stressed." Last month it was your haircut, and before that your new job title.
I'm not going to tell you what to do. I only noticed that you go quiet after those calls, and it made me sad, because at work you're the one everyone trusts to sort things out.
If you ever want to talk, or just want company while you think, my phone is on. No lecture, promise. And if it ever feels bigger than a friend can help with, I'll happily go with you to see a counsellor.
Lavanya

qa.q: What did Dev say about Ritu on the call during the team lunch?
qa.a: He said Ritu was "too dumb to book a cab".

qa.q: Why did Lavanya choose to write once instead of arguing the point?
qa.a: Lavanya felt worried and sad for Ritu, but also cautious, sensing that pushing hard could make Ritu defensive, so naming it once felt kinder.

qa.q: Which part of Lavanya's approach is wise?
qa.a: Naming one specific moment gently, not demanding a decision, and staying available, even offering to go to a counsellor together, keeps the door open without a fight.

qa.q: How might Ritu feel reading the email?
qa.a: Ritu might feel embarrassed or defensive at first, yet also noticed and less alone, knowing someone saw the pattern without judging.

grounding: A colleague notices a friend brushing off a partner's repeated put-downs as just his way, names it gently once, and stays available.

passage:
The week before Holi break, the classroom smelled faintly of the gulal someone had smuggled in.
"Kiran, can you read question four?" Ms Thomas asked.
Kiran's pencil clattered to the floor. "Me? Um. Yes, Miss."
At lunch, Ganga nudged him. "Why do you jump every time she says your name?"
"I don't jump."
"You do. Ever since that assembly in December. When you said the pledge wrong on the mic and everyone laughed?"
Kiran frowned, honestly puzzled. "What assembly? I've never been on the mic."
"You have! Your ears went red and—"
"Ganga, I don't remember that." He pushed his lunchbox away. "Can we talk about Holi colours instead?"
Ganga studied him for a moment, then shrugged. "Okay. Green or pink?"

qa.q: What happened at the December assembly, according to Ganga?
qa.a: Kiran said the pledge wrong on the mic and everyone laughed.

qa.q: What might Kiran be feeling when Ms Thomas calls his name?
qa.a: Probably a sudden jolt of fear and shame from the forgotten assembly; the memory is gone, but the humiliated feeling still makes him jump.

qa.q: How could Ms Thomas support Kiran in class?
qa.a: She could give him a quiet heads-up before calling on him and notice small tries, so speaking in class slowly feels safe again.

qa.q: Why might Ganga react by changing the subject?
qa.a: Ganga sees that pushing upsets Kiran, so she chooses kindness over proving she is right, even though she remembers clearly.

grounding: A child cannot recall being laughed at in assembly, yet still flinches when the teacher calls on him.

passage:
Navratri rehearsals had taken over the school hall. Pallavi was fine through the first two songs, laughing as Vishal tripped over his own dandiya sticks. Then the third track began, an old film song with a slow flute opening. Pallavi's shoulders went stiff. She stopped mid-step and stood by the wall, arms folded, jaw tight.
"You okay?" Vishal asked.
"Yeah. I just don't like this one."
"Why? Didn't your family play it at your cousin's engagement last year? You told me there was some big fight that night."
Pallavi frowned. "Was there? I honestly don't remember much. Someone shouted, I think." She stared at the speaker until the song ended, then picked her sticks back up as if nothing had happened.

qa.q: Which song made Pallavi stop dancing?
qa.a: The third track, an old film song with a slow flute opening.

qa.q: What does Pallavi's stiff body suggest when the song begins?
qa.a: She seems tense and hurt, as if the feeling from the family fight is still stored even though she honestly cannot recall the details.

qa.q: What small step could help Pallavi?
qa.a: She could notice which songs or places make her tense and, when she is ready, talk about that night with a trusted adult or the school counsellor.

qa.q: How does Vishal see Pallavi's reaction?
qa.a: He is puzzled and a little concerned, because he remembers her mentioning a big fight, yet she seems genuinely not to remember it.

grounding: A teenager remembers little of a bitter family fight but goes rigid whenever the song from that night plays.

passage:
Afreen and I have shared a hostel room since first year, so I thought I knew all her moods. Last Sunday I lit a mosquito coil because the monsoon bugs were terrible. Within a minute she was standing by the door, rigid, snapping, "Put that out. Now." I did. She spent the next hour banging drawers. Then at dinner a senior joked, "Stop being so dramatic," and she went pale and left her plate.
I don't know what those two things mean to her, and it isn't my place to guess. Later I just said, "Hey, I noticed the coil bothered you. I won't light it again. And if you ever want to talk, I'm around."
She nodded. "Thanks, Jeevan," she said, and switched off the light.

qa.q: What did Jeevan light that bothered Afreen?
qa.a: A mosquito coil.

qa.q: What was Jeevan feeling after Afreen snapped about the coil?
qa.a: Jeevan felt puzzled and a bit stung, but also concerned, and chose not to guess at a story Afreen had not shared.

qa.q: Which choice by Jeevan worked, and why?
qa.a: Naming the reaction kindly, promising not to light the coil again and offering to listen without asking for reasons respected Afreen's privacy 🙂.

qa.q: What might it be like for Afreen when a certain smell or phrase hits her?
qa.a: It may feel sudden and overwhelming, and she may not be able to explain it even to herself, so being pushed for reasons could make it worse.

grounding: A roommate notices a friend react sharply to a smell and a phrase, and responds kindly without digging for a story.

passage:
Ward note, maternity wing, Pongal week.
Anjali's brother, Karthik, visited this afternoon with sugarcane stalks for the new mother. When I placed the baby girl in his arms, he smiled for a moment, then his face crumpled. He handed her back quickly and stood at the window, shoulders shaking.
Afterwards he told me, embarrassed, that their mother died when he was four, a week after a Pongal just like this one. "I haven't thought about her properly in twenty years. I thought I was over it." Anjali held his hand and said she had felt the same during labour.
I sat with them for a while, told Karthik that feelings like this often come back at births, and gave him the hospital counsellor's number in case the grief keeps returning.

qa.q: What did Karthik bring when he visited the maternity wing?
qa.a: Sugarcane stalks for the new mother.

qa.q: Why was Karthik embarrassed after he cried?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and caught off guard, because he believed he was over his mother's death, and holding the baby flooded him with grief he thought was long gone.

qa.q: How could Karthik look after himself in the coming weeks?
qa.a: He could let himself talk about their mother with Anjali, and use the counsellor's number if the grief keeps returning or feels too heavy.

qa.q: How is Anjali affected by seeing Karthik cry?
qa.a: She understands him because she felt the same during labour, and holding his hand shows the shared loss drawing them closer.

grounding: A young adult holding a newborn is suddenly flooded with grief for a mother lost in early childhood.

passage:
Last month, clearing out Nani's old trunk, I found my Class 5 report card, from the year Papa left. The teacher's comment said: "Payal has become very quiet." I sat on the floor and something in my chest cracked open.
My old habit would have been to shut the trunk, put on a podcast and clean the whole flat. This time I let myself cry. Then I wrote two pages about that year in my notebook, messy and unfair and true. That evening I called Gurleen and read one paragraph aloud. She didn't try to fix anything; she just said, "That sounds so lonely."
It still aches sometimes. So I've booked a session with a counsellor for next week, because I'd rather not carry this alone again.

qa.q: What did Payal find in Nani's trunk?
qa.a: The Class 5 report card from the year Papa left.

qa.q: Why did Payal choose to cry instead of shutting the trunk?
qa.a: Payal felt an old, deep sadness and chose to let it be felt rather than bury it again, sensing that pushing it down had never really worked.

qa.q: Which steps helped Payal handle the old hurt?
qa.a: Crying, writing about that year, reading a paragraph aloud to Gurleen, and booking a counsellor because the ache keeps coming back.

qa.q: How might Gurleen feel hearing that paragraph?
qa.a: Gurleen probably feels moved and trusted, and chooses to listen and name the loneliness instead of rushing to fix it.

grounding: An adult lets an old childhood hurt be felt, written down and shared with a trusted person, and books a counsellor when it keeps aching.

passage:
Before: On the first cold morning of the winter holidays, Anand grabbed Jaya's toy train on the verandah. When she reached for it, he shouted, "You're being mean! You're so angry!" His own fists were tight.
During: Two days later, at their Nani's house, Jaya only looked at the train, and Anand yelled, "Stop being cross at me!"
After: On Sunday, Mummy knelt beside him. "I think Anand feels cross right now." Anand stamped his foot. Then he mumbled, "Me cross," and pushed the train back to Jaya.

qa.q: Where did Anand first grab Jaya's toy train?
qa.a: On the verandah.

qa.q: Why did Anand shout that Jaya was angry?
qa.a: He was angry himself 😠, with tight fists, but owning that feeling was too uncomfortable, so he put it onto Jaya instead.

qa.q: How did Mummy help, and what could she keep doing?
qa.a: She calmly named Anand's feeling without blaming him, which let him say "Me cross"; she can keep putting words to his feelings.

qa.q: What is it like for Jaya to be called mean?
qa.a: It is confusing and unfair, because she only reached for or looked at her own train and gets blamed for anger that is not hers.

grounding: A young child who snatched a toy accuses the other child of being mean and angry, placing his own anger outside himself.

subtype: Accusing a friend of the child's own envy [Actor]
passage:
"Amma, Sharmila came to school with a new bag today. Purple, with a unicorn zip."
"Nice. First day after the summer holidays, everyone wants something new."
"She's showing off. She kept putting it on the desk so everyone could see."
"Where else would she put it?"
"She's jealous of everyone, Amma. That's why she needs fancy things."
"Who is she jealous of?"
"Everyone! She looked at my water bottle."
Amma glanced at Pooja's old blue bag, its strap tied in a knot. "Did you like the purple one?"
"No." Pooja kicked the bag under the table. "Unicorns are for babies." She was quiet for a moment. "Can mine get fixed before the rains?"

qa.q: What was Sharmila's new bag like?
qa.a: Purple, with a unicorn zip.

qa.q: Why does Pooja insist that Sharmila is jealous of everyone?
qa.a: Pooja feels envious of the new bag, but that feeling is uncomfortable, so she sees jealousy in Sharmila instead of in herself.

qa.q: How could Amma help Pooja?
qa.a: Amma could gently say it is okay to wish for a new bag 🙂, then talk about fixing the old strap, so Pooja can own the wish without shame.

qa.q: How might Sharmila feel if she heard what Pooja said?
qa.a: She would probably be hurt and puzzled, since she was only using her new bag the way anyone would.

grounding: A child who envies a classmate's new bag accuses the classmate of showing off and being jealous.

passage:
Before: The Monday after the Durga Puja holidays, Jahnavi walked into class with her new short haircut and kept her head down. She was sure the whole back row went silent. When Chetan glanced up, she heard, in her head, "That looks awful."
During: On Wednesday she wore a cap until the teacher asked her to take it off. Every giggle in the room felt like it was about her fringe. She texted her cousin: "Everyone hates it. I look ridiculous 😔"
After: On Friday, during group work, Chetan said, "Oh, you cut your hair? It's nice." Jahnavi blinked. "You weren't laughing on Monday?" "I was laughing at Mohit's lunch." She realised the harshest voice had been her own, and it was still there, just a little quieter.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi wear to class on Wednesday?
qa.a: A cap, until the teacher asked her to take it off.

qa.q: Why was Jahnavi so sure that Chetan thought her haircut looked awful?
qa.a: She felt insecure and self-critical about her looks, and heard her own harsh judgement as if it came from him.

qa.q: What could Jahnavi try when she feels the whole class is staring?
qa.a: Check the facts, for example by noticing what people are really laughing at, and treat the harsh inner voice as a thought rather than proof.

qa.q: How does Chetan see Jahnavi's haircut?
qa.a: He hardly noticed it at first and then thinks it is nice; on Monday he was laughing at Mohit's lunch, not at her.

grounding: A teenager unsure about her looks after a haircut feels sure the class is judging her, when the criticism is her own.

subtype: Being accused of hostility one does not feel [Receiver]
passage:
The fight happened on Holi, of all days. I'd come home tired from playing colours and gone straight to the shower. When I came out, my flatmate Yamini was standing in the kitchen. "You've been cold to me for weeks, Deepak. Just admit you're angry."
I wasn't. I'd been buried in exams. For a second I almost apologised for a feeling I didn't have. Instead I sat down and asked, "Which moments felt cold?" She named two: I skipped her birthday dinner for a lab, and I left one of her messages unanswered. Both true, and I said sorry for those.
Then, quietly, she admitted she was still upset about the rent split from last term. Looking back, the anger in that kitchen was real. It just wasn't mine.

qa.q: Which two moments did Yamini name as cold?
qa.a: Deepak skipped her birthday dinner for a lab and left one of her messages unanswered.

qa.q: What was Deepak feeling when Yamini said "Just admit you're angry"?
qa.a: Deepak felt confused and briefly guilty, almost apologising for a feeling that was not there, before choosing to stay calm.

qa.q: What worked about how Deepak responded?
qa.a: Asking for specific moments let Deepak apologise for the real lapses without accepting the whole charge, and it gave Yamini room to name her own grudge.

qa.q: What might Yamini have been feeling underneath her accusation?
qa.a: She was still upset about the rent split, and it was easier to see anger in Deepak than to face her own resentment.

grounding: A student accused by a flatmate of hidden anger calmly checks the facts and finds the grudge belongs to the flatmate.
